title: Rate Limiter
summary: Limit how often a client may call an API, across many servers.
problem: Design a rate limiting service that protects APIs from abuse: for example, 100 requests per minute per API key.
functional: Limit by user, API key or IP, with different rules per endpoint
Tell the client when it is limited and when to retry
Rules can be changed without a deploy
nonFunctional: Adds under 5 ms to a request
Works correctly across many API servers
If the limiter fails the API keeps working (fail open) or is protected (fail closed): decide and justify
constraints: A million requests per second at peak
deliverables: Requirements and the assumptions you made
A capacity estimate (requests per second, storage, bandwidth)
A high-level architecture diagram (Mermaid or an uploaded image)
The API (endpoints and payloads) and the data model
How it scales, how it fails, and what you would monitor
The main trade-offs and what you chose not to build
hints: Compare fixed window, sliding window and token bucket.
Where does the shared counter live, and what happens to concurrent updates?
reference:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
  C[Client] --> GW[API gateway with limiter middleware]
  GW -->|check and decrement| R[(Redis: counters / token buckets)]
  GW -->|allowed| S[Service]
  GW -->|limited| X[429 + Retry-After]
  Cfg[(Rules store)] --> GW
```

- **Algorithms.** Fixed window is the cheapest (one counter) but allows up to twice the limit across a window boundary. A sliding window log is exact but stores every request time. A sliding window counter approximates it with two counters. A **token bucket** per key allows bursts up to the bucket size while holding the average rate; it stores two numbers (tokens, last refill time) and is the one used here. Choose by whether bursts are acceptable and how exact the limit must be.
- **Capacity (assumptions).** At 1 million checks per second, one Redis node (very roughly 100,000 simple operations per second; measure yours) is far from enough, so plan on tens of shards with replicas, and note that every request pays one network round trip to Redis, which is why the 5 ms budget matters. A local per-server counter that syncs periodically cuts that cost but lets the limit be overshot by a margin; that is the trade-off against exactness.
- The check-and-update must be **atomic**: a Lua script or a single Redis command per request, so concurrent servers do not both spend the last token. Take the time from Redis (`TIME`) rather than from each API server, so clock skew between servers does not distort the refill.
- Respond **429** with `Retry-After` and `X-RateLimit-Remaining` headers.
- Rules are cached at the gateway and refreshed from the rules store, so changes need no deploy.
- Shard counters by key across Redis nodes; for the limiter failing, **fail open** for general APIs and **fail closed** for sensitive ones such as login.
